[Mosaic is a benchmark for differentiable solvers. It measures whether they are fit for purpose and at what cost, in compute and in development effort. Because every solver runs the same setups under the same protocol, Mosaic also allows researchers to investigate patterns across solvers, for example between solvers that share numerical characteristics, or between gradient quality and optimization performance. [Our paper](paper.qmd) is one such investigation.]{.hero-lede}

::: {.hero-actions}

## What Mosaic measures {#what-mosaic-measures}

If you train a model or run an optimizer through a simulation, the solver has to return a correct prediction (the *forward* pass) and a usable gradient of that prediction with respect to your inputs (the vector–Jacobian product, VJP). A solver that runs fast and predicts accurately is of little use for gradient-based work if its VJP is wrong, noisy or ill-conditioned, so Mosaic checks both. Every solver is asked to compute an output $y = f(x)$ and the VJP $\bar{x} = (\partial f / \partial x)^\top \bar{y}$ on each setup it supports, and the results answer three questions:

::: {.axis-row}
::: {.axis-card style="--tile: var(--m-indigo)"}
[Is the solver fit for purpose?]{.axis-q}

Forward, gradient and optimization checks, the reliability of each solver across a setup's experiments, and its deviations from the setup.
:::
::: {.axis-card style="--tile: var(--m-accent)"}
[At what cost?]{.axis-q}

Wall-clock time and peak memory of the forward and VJP calls, and the development effort it took to make the solver run the setup.
:::
::: {.axis-card style="--tile: var(--m-saffron)"}
[Which patterns hold across solvers?]{.axis-q}

Comparisons across solvers that share a discretization or AD strategy, or between gradient quality and optimization performance.
:::
:::

The [results overview](results.qmd) reports the first two for every solver on every setup. Patterns are not a column of their own. The overview's section on [investigating patterns](results.qmd#investigating-patterns) points at the data and the solver metadata to start from, and the [paper](paper.qmd) is a worked example.

### Effort and deviations

A check that passes says little about how much work it took to get there. Every solver therefore keeps an intervention record in its `tesseract_config.yaml`, listing everything that was done beyond using the library as intended, with the reason on each setup, the evidence and any upstream issue. The effort a solver needs on a setup is the highest level among the interventions it requires there:

- **L0**, nothing beyond expected tweaks, meaning the public API with its defaults or documented options, such as a solver tolerance.
- **L1**, undocumented configuration.
- **L2**, user code on the library's public primitives.
- **L3**, changing the solver itself.

Deviations record where a solver runs a substitute for part of the prescribed setup, such as a different outflow condition, together with the effect on its results. Effort and deviations sit next to the checks on every results page, and the [solver reference](solvers.qmd) lists each intervention in full.

## Terminology {#terminology}

The results and the rest of these docs use five terms with a fixed meaning.

Domain
: A family of solvers that share one canonical schema and one directory under `mosaic/tesseracts/`. There are three: `navier-stokes-grid`, `structural-mesh` and `thermal-mesh`.

Problem
: The benchmark package selected with `mosaic run -p`, which registers experiments and their settings. There are four: `ns-grid`, `ns-3d-grid`, `structural-mesh` and `thermal-mesh`. Both Navier–Stokes problems use the `navier-stokes-grid` domain. You only need this term to run the benchmark or contribute to it.

Setup
: A problem statement that results are reported for, such as channel flow past a cylinder. There are six, shown [above](#setups). A problem can have several setups, and every experiment belongs to exactly one. Checks, effort and deviations are reported per setup.

Solver
: One Tesseract under a domain directory, wrapping one library. A solver can serve several problems and setups. The `navier-stokes-grid` solvers serve both Navier–Stokes problems.

Backend
: The runtime or AD framework a solver is built on, such as JAX or PyTorch, as recorded in its `metadata.mosaic.backend`.

## Evaluation protocol {#evaluation-protocol}

Each solver is wrapped in a Docker container by [tesseract-core](https://github.com/pasteurlabs/tesseract-core), which exposes a uniform `apply` / `vjp` interface. The harness calls those containers as JAX functions through [tesseract-jax](https://github.com/pasteurlabs/tesseract-jax), so it can compare solvers built on incompatible AD frameworks (JAX, PyTorch, Julia, hand-written C++ adjoints) without a shared dependency. The protocol is solver-agnostic. It only uses `apply` and `vjp`, and never inspects how a solver computes its gradient.

The settings of every experiment (grid sizes, sweep ranges, finite-difference steps, iteration caps and pass criteria) live next to it in the problem configurations under [`mosaic/benchmarks/problems/`](https://github.com/pasteurlabs/mosaic/tree/main/mosaic/benchmarks/problems), and each [results page](results.qmd) describes the experiments of its setup.

**Forward accuracy.** Resolution sweeps against a reference: an analytic solution where one exists (the 2D Taylor–Green vortex, the laminar Kolmogorov shear flow), the Schäfer–Turek literature value for the cylinder, converged high-resolution spectral runs for the 3D Taylor–Green vortex and the turbulent Kolmogorov flow, and for the mesh setups the trimmed mean of all solvers, stored as a precomputed reference. Where it applies, the suite also checks physical laws such as a divergence-free velocity field.

**Gradient accuracy.** Central finite differences through the Tesseract interface serve as the solver-agnostic ground truth. For a scalar loss of the output, the harness compares the VJP's directional derivatives $d^\text{ad}_k = \langle g, v_k \rangle$ along random directions $v_k$ with central-difference estimates $d^\text{fd}_k$ along the same directions. It reports the cosine similarity between the vectors $d^\text{ad}$ and $d^\text{fd}$ (direction agreement, $1$ is identical) and the median over directions of $|d^\text{ad}_k - d^\text{fd}_k| / \max(|d^\text{ad}_k|, |d^\text{fd}_k|)$ (magnitude agreement, $0$ is exact). The step size $\varepsilon$ is swept relative to the magnitude of the input, and the check uses the best $\varepsilon$, which avoids both the truncation regime (large $\varepsilon$) and the round-off regime (small $\varepsilon$). Depending on the setup, the gradient suite also compares against analytic gradients, follows the gradient error as a physical parameter or the rollout length grows, differentiates through a chain of solver calls, and inspects the singular-value spectrum of the Jacobian, where a wide spread signals an ill-conditioned gradient that can stall an optimizer.

**Optimization.** Each optimization setup runs a gradient-based optimizer (L-BFGS or Adam, depending on the setup) through the solver up to an iteration cap. The check passes when the objective falls below a set fraction of its initial value. Drag minimization also requires the final drag to land close to the other solvers' median. This catches solvers whose gradients pass the finite-difference check but still fail to drive a full optimization.

**Cost.** Forward and VJP wall-clock time and peak memory, swept over problem size and rollout length on each solver's hardware target. Each sweep point starts with an untimed warm-up call, which covers compilation, followed by repeated timed trials.

## Benchmark suites {#suites}

Experiments are grouped into suites, which you select with `mosaic run --suites`. Each [results page](results.qmd) lists the experiments of its setup.

| Suite | What it does |
|:------|:-------------|
| `forward` | Forward accuracy against references, and physical-law checks |
| `gradient` | Gradients against finite differences and analytic solutions, gradient behavior across parameters and rollout lengths, and Jacobian spectra |
| `optimization` | Gradient-based optimization through the solver |
| `cost` | Forward and VJP wall-clock time and peak memory across problem sizes and rollout lengths |
| `ics` | Generates and plots the initial conditions, without running a solver |

A run writes metrics as JSON, fields as NPZ, and plots as PNG with a Vega-Lite `.vl.json` spec next to each, under `mosaic-results/<problem>/<suite>/<experiment>/`. [Reading the output](getting-started.qmd#reading-the-output) explains the layout.
